newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli, PLO leaders leave door open for summit.
newsitem.headline: Israeli, PLO leaders leave door open for summit.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat left the door open to a summit meeting on Tuesday but each set conditions, underscoring the crisis in Middle East peacemaking.

In the West Bank towns of Bethlehem and Hebron, Palestinian stone-throwers clashed with Israeli troops who fired teargas and rubber bullets on a sixth day of violence sparked by Netanyahu's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Arafat, on a visit to the Sri Lankan capital of Colombo, said he was prepared to meet Prime Minister Netanyahu so long as the purpose of their meeting was to discuss peace and not a publicity stunt.
"Why not? If this is for peace I am ready, but if it is for propaganda, it is something different," Arafat told reporters.
U.S. officials said a peace mission by Middle East negotiator Dennis Ross was under consideration but far from set.
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan said the prime minister would accept a summit with Arafat so long as the issue of security topped the agenda.
"We are obviously not rejecting any idea for a meeting but we expect that if such a meeting takes place, it will focus on the issues of security and terrorism," Bar-Illan told Reuters.
Palestinians object to any preconditions and say the sides must talk about other issues besides security.

The Palestinians deny charges by Netanyahu that Arafat has given Islamic militants a tacit "green light" to carry out attacks, including a Palestinian's suicide bombing that killed three women at a Tel Aviv cafe last week.
In Jerusalem, Israel's army chief Amnon Shahak said on Tuesday: "The ground is obviously fertile for more attacks ... We are in a very tense situation."

Ending a visit to Sri Lanka, Arafat said his Palestinian Authority had acted against those who opposed the law, including the main Islamic militant group Hamas. He accused Israel of fomenting confrontation between Palestinian groups.

"The Israeli government is looking to having instability and confrontation between the Palestinians, a civil war, which we cannot accept," Arafat said when asked about Israel's demand that he clamp down on militant groups.

Arafat's Fatah movement, angry at the building of 6,500 homes for Jews, called on Palestinians to confront Jewish settlement activity with non-violent protests and by blocking roads used by Jewish settlers in the West Bank.
"Our objective is to raise our voice to the world against settlement activity. But we are not calling for violence," Fatah spokesman Mahmoud Jasser told Reuters.

On Monday, Mohammad Dahlan, the head of Palestinian Preventive Security in Gaza, said he had stopped security coordination with Israel. Netanyahu's adviser Dore Gold said the only possible security contacts were at a low level.

Ross, the U.S. Middle East peace envoy, underscored in an interview with the MSNBC cable television network the need "for 100 percent effort" in fighting terrorism and said: "We'd like to see them (the Palestinians) do more."
Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy appealed to Arafat this week to cut short his eight-day trip abroad and return to Gaza to deal with the deepening crisis.
Police arrested three Israeli Arabs on suspicion they helped the suicide bomber enter Israel from the West Bank, Israeli army radio said, adding the three had denied the accusations.
